content: Neuroblastoma is a pediatric embryonic tumor that originates from the neural crest. It is the second most common extracranial malignant solid tumor in children. Neuroblastoma cells have a unique ability to take up Iodine-123-metaiodobenzylguanidine (¹²³I-MIBG), which allows for imaging of the tumor. The use of ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy is critical not only for diagnosing neuroblastoma but also for staging the disease and identifying skeletal lesions. When skeletal lesions are present, follow-up MIBG scans are employed to evaluate the patient’s response to therapy. However, the sensitivity and specificity of ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy for detecting neuroblastoma vary across studies. Prognosis, treatment planning, and therapeutic response in neuroblastoma patients are often based on extension scoring derived from ¹²³I-MIBG scans. Given its clinical significance, it is essential to determine the precise diagnostic accuracy of ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy. In cases where the tumor does not exhibit MIBG avidity, fluorine-18-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) is frequently utilized, and its diagnostic accuracy also warrants evaluation. The primary objectives of this study were to assess the diagnostic accuracy of ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy (using single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), with or without computed tomography (CT)) for detecting neuroblastoma and its metastases at initial diagnosis or recurrence in children aged 0 to 18 years. Additionally, the study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging as an add-on test in cases of negative ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy. Secondary objectives included determining the diagnostic accuracy of 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging as a standalone test for detecting neuroblastoma and its metastases, as well as comparing the diagnostic accuracy of ¹²³I-MIBG (SPECT-CT) scintigraphy and 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging. The search strategy involved querying databases such as MEDLINE/PubMed and EMBASE for relevant articles published up to September 11, 2012. Reference lists of pertinent articles, conference proceedings, and unpublished studies were also reviewed. Studies included in the analysis were cross-sectional or case series involving children aged 0 to 18 years with histologically confirmed neuroblastoma, either at initial diagnosis or recurrence. These studies compared the results of ¹²³I-MIBG (SPECT-CT) scintigraphy and/or 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging with reference standards or with each other. Data extraction and analysis were conducted by two independent reviewers. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated using two-by-two tables that included the number of true positive and false negative results. Forest plots were generated to display sensitivity and specificity estimates with 95% confidence intervals when possible. Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria. Ten studies reported data at the patient level, indicating whether the scan was positive or negative, while one study reported data at the lesion level. The sensitivity of ¹²³I-MIBG (SPECT-CT) scintigraphy for detecting neuroblastoma (objective 1.1) ranged from 67% to 100% across 608 of 621 eligible patients. Specificity data were available from one study, which reported a specificity of 68% based on 115 lesions in 22 patients. For detecting metastases separately from the primary tumor, the sensitivity of ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy ranged from 79% to 100% in three studies, while specificity ranged from 33% to 89% in two studies. One study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging as an add-on test in patients with negative ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy (objective 1.2). Among 24 eligible patients with confirmed neuroblastoma, two had negative ¹²³I-MIBG scans but positive 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) scans. The sensitivity of 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging as a standalone diagnostic test (objective 2.1) and in comparison to ¹²³I-MIBG (SPECT-CT) scintigraphy (objective 2.2) was reported in one study. The sensitivity of 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging was 100%, compared to 92% for ¹²³I-MIBG (SPECT-CT) scintigraphy. Specificity could not be calculated for either modality due to insufficient data. The sensitivity of ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy for detecting neuroblastoma and its metastases ranged from 67% to 100% in patients with histologically confirmed neuroblastoma. However, false positive findings, though rarely reported, can occur. For instance, physiological uptake must be excluded using SPECT-CT scans, but further research is needed to draw definitive conclusions. Approximately 10% of patients with histologically confirmed neuroblastoma do not exhibit MIBG avidity, resulting in false negative findings. For these patients, additional tests, such as 18F-FDG-PET(-CT), are recommended for staging and assessing therapeutic response. However, more evidence is required to confirm the clinical utility of 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging in this context. The limited data available precluded the calculation of diagnostic accuracy for 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging in cases of negative ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy. Similarly, the diagnostic accuracy of 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) imaging for detecting neuroblastoma and its metastases, as well as its comparison to ¹²³I-MIBG (SPECT-CT) scintigraphy, could not be determined due to insufficient data. The authors suggest that the term sensitivity to assess the presence of neuroblastoma may be more appropriate than diagnostic accuracy for the study objectives, given the limited specificity data available.
